⭐ STAR #1 — SQL Analysis:
❓ Q: Tell me about a time you used SQL to solve a complex data problem
In a portfolio project analyzing e-commerce transactions, I explored customer behavior across regions. My goal was to identify high-performing segments and surface actionable revenue insights.
I used SQL to join multiple datasets — customers, orders, and products. I calculated key metrics such as average order value, total revenue per region, and customer frequency. I also used CASE WHEN to segment high-value customers and applied ROW_NUMBER() to rank customers within regions.
Result:
I found that 20% of regions drove 60% of revenue — a classic 80/20 split. That kind of concentration means a marketing team can focus spend on a small number of high-value regions for outsized return. I documented the full analysis as a business case with a projected +12% conversion lift.

⭐ STAR #10 — Data Quality Engineering (M:
❓ Q: Tell me about a time you found a bug that was hard to detect
I was building a data quality agent with 19 analysis tools connected to real portfolio databases. During QA testing, I noticed that time series analysis was silently returning dates from 1970 instead of raising an error.
My goal was to identify the root cause and fix it properly — not just patch the symptom.
The bug was subtle: the column contained integer years (2024, 2025), but the tool was parsing them as nanosecond timestamps. Because 1970 is a valid date and not NULL, the standard dropna() check passed silently — the bug survived all basic validation.
I introduced a _validate_date_col() helper that blocks integer columns from being used as date inputs. The key decision was to fix the class of failure, not just one instance. The same helper covered two tools at once: both time_series and freshness_check.
I then validated the fix using a 33-test suite structured in A/B/C/D blocks — routing, edge cases, error handling, and cross-tool consistency. All 33 tests passed.
💥 Golden Interview Line:
I don't just patch the symptom — I find the class of failure and close all instances.
Follow-up thinking:
• The fix was reusable across all future tools that accept date columns
• Silent failures are more dangerous than loud ones
• Validation at the boundary is better than checking at each call site
